title: Be Strong and Courageous
subtitle: Joshua & Judges in Poems & Pictures
author: Timothy Holt
beforeYouBegin: Joshua begins with a man told three times to be strong, standing where Moses used to stand. Then come a scarlet line tied in a window, priests stepping into a river in flood, twelve stones carried up from the riverbed, the last morning of manna, seven trumpets of rams' horns, an old man asking for the hard hill country, and a people told to choose today whom they will serve. Judges begins with a generation that forgot, and goes round and round: a woman judging under a palm tree, a farmer threshing wheat in a winepress, a fleece wet with dew, torches hidden in clay jars, a strong man whose hair began to grow again, and a last prayer between two pillars.

parts.title: Be Strong and Courageous
parts.epigraph: Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid.
parts.lightHint: Beside the twelve wet river stones stacked near the reeds of the bank

parts.title: Not One Thing Has Failed
parts.epigraph: Not one thing has failed of all the good things which Yahweh your God spoke concerning you.
parts.lightHint: Under the ancient oak of Shechem beside the great witness stone

parts.title: Another Generation
parts.epigraph: Another generation arose after them who didn’t know Yahweh.
parts.lightHint: In the shade of the hill-country palm tree between Ramah and Bethel

parts.title: Mighty Man of Valor
parts.epigraph: Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!
parts.lightHint: Where the clay pitcher shatters to let the hidden torchlight blaze

parts.title: Remember Me
parts.epigraph: Remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once.
parts.lightHint: Near the olive and fig trees before the Finale Plaza

paintings.title: after Moses
paintings.epigraph: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you nor forsake you.”
paintings.poem:
Moses is dead.
that is how it starts.

the one who talked with God
like a friend,
the one who held the staff
over the sea,
gone.

and now it's you.

three times God says it:
be strong.
be strong.
be strong and courageous.

not because you are.
because he is
going with you,
the same as before.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “after Moses” (Joshua 1:1–9), what would you talk about after reading, “because he is going with you, the same as before”?

paintings.title: day and night
paintings.epigraph: “you shall meditate on it day and night”
paintings.poem:
before the river,
before the walls,
a book.

keep it in your mouth,
he said.
turn it over
at noon,
turn it over
by lamplight.

the land was ahead.
the way into it
was words.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the moving water: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “day and night”—“the way into it was words”?

paintings.title: the scarlet line
paintings.epigraph: “Then she tied the scarlet line in the window.”
paintings.poem:
she had heard the stories.
the sea,
the kings across the river.

everyone in Jericho had heard.
their hearts melted.

hers did something else.

your God, she said,
is God in heaven above
and on the earth beneath.

a woman on the wall,
with the wrong past
and the right answer,

tying a red thread
to her window
like a knot in a promise:

remember me.
remember my house.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the moving water in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “a woman on the wall, with the wrong past and the right answer, tying a red thread to her window like a knot in a promise: remember me. remember my house” (Joshua 2:8–21)?

paintings.title: this way before
paintings.epigraph: “for you have not passed this way before.”
paintings.poem:
keep your distance
from the ark, they were told.
not so you'd be far from God.

so you could see
where it was going.

you have not passed
this way before.

none of us have.
that's why we follow
something we can see
a long way off.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Joshua 3:1–6, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “this way before”—and ends with, “that's why we follow something we can see a long way off.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: the edge of the water
paintings.epigraph: “the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water”
paintings.poem:
it was harvest.
the river was over its banks.

of course it was.

nothing moved
until someone's feet
were wet.

then, far upstream,
the water stood still
in a heap,

and the priests
stood in the middle
on dry ground

until every last one
had crossed.

sometimes the miracle
waits for your sandal
to touch the flood.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Joshua 3:14–17 points us to the moving water and whispers, “sometimes the miracle waits for your sandal to touch the flood.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: what these stones mean
paintings.epigraph: “What do these stones mean?”
paintings.poem:
twelve men
waded back into the riverbed
and each one
lifted a stone
to his shoulder.

wet stones.
heavy stones.
from the place
where the priests had stood.

stack them, God said,
where you camp tonight.

one day a child
will put a hand on them
and ask.

and you will get to say,
we walked through here
on dry ground.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “and you will get to say, we walked through here on dry ground.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the last morning of manna
paintings.epigraph: “The manna ceased on the next day, after they had eaten of the produce of the land.”
paintings.poem:
forty years
of bread on the ground
every morning.

then one day
they ate the grain of the land,
roasted,

and the next morning
there was none.

no one had announced it.
no one had to.

the God who fed them
in the desert
was feeding them now
with fields.

same hands.
different bread.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “same hands. different bread” (Joshua 5:10–12) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: holy ground
paintings.epigraph: “Take off your sandals, for the place on which you stand is holy.”
paintings.poem:
are you for us
or for our enemies?

a fair question
outside Jericho.

no, came the answer.

not on your side.
in charge.

so Joshua did the only thing
that made sense.

he took off his sandals.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “holy ground” (Joshua 5:13–15): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “in charge. he took off his sandals”?

paintings.title: seven days of silence
paintings.epigraph: “You shall not shout nor let your voice be heard”
paintings.poem:
once around.
back to camp.

once around.
back to camp.

six days of walking
past a locked city
without a word.

only the rams' horns
and the sound of feet.

it must have felt foolish.
it must have felt like nothing.

some obedience
is just keeping quiet
and going around again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Joshua 6:1–16 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “some obedience is just keeping quiet and going around again” in your own story?

paintings.title: the wall fell down flat
paintings.epigraph: “the wall fell down flat”
paintings.poem:
the seventh day.
seven times around.

then the long blast,
and the shout
they had been holding
for a week,

and the stones
that had never moved
for anyone

lay down.

not pushed.
not climbed.

just
told.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “the wall fell down flat” (Joshua 6:15–20), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the stones of the wall after reading, “not pushed. not climbed. just told”?

paintings.title: in the middle of Israel
paintings.epigraph: “She lives in the middle of Israel to this day”
paintings.poem:
when the dust settled
there was one window
still tied with red.

they brought her out,
and her father,
and her mother,
and her brothers,
and all she had.

the outsider
from the wall

now living
in the middle
of the people of God.

that was always
how the story
was meant to go.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“when the dust settled there was one window still tied with red”) and the closing thought (“that was always how the story was meant to go”), what is Joshua 6:22–25 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: hidden in the ground
paintings.epigraph: “Tell me now what you have done! Don’t hide it from me!”
paintings.poem:
a beautiful robe.
some silver.
a bar of gold.

I saw them, I wanted them,
I took them, I hid them.
the oldest four steps there are.

my son, Joshua said,
don't hide it from me.

they raised a heap of stones
in the valley of Achor,
the valley of trouble.

much later, a prophet heard God promise
to make that same valley
a door of hope.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Be Strong and Courageous, “hidden in the ground” (Joshua 7:19–26) slows us down at the open threshold to remind us: “much later, a prophet heard God promise to make that same valley a door of hope.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: the little ones and the foreigners
paintings.epigraph: “with the women, the little ones, and the foreigners who were among them.”
paintings.poem:
he read all of it.
every word.

not only to the elders.
not only to the men.

to the women.
to the little ones.
to the foreigners
standing at the edges.

no one was too small
or too new
to hear what God had said.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “the little ones and the foreigners” (Joshua 8:30–35), what would you talk about after reading, “no one was too small or too new to hear what God had said”?

paintings.title: the day the sun stood still
paintings.epigraph: “There was no day like that before it or after it, that Yahweh listened to the voice of a man”
paintings.poem:
sun, stand still,
he said.

and the sun
stayed in the middle of the sky.

the text doesn't marvel
at the sun.

it marvels
at this:

God listened
to the voice
of a man.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the still, unhurried voice: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “the day the sun stood still”—“it marvels at this: God listened to the voice of a man”?

paintings.title: give me this hill country
paintings.epigraph: “Now therefore give me this hill country”
paintings.poem:
forty years old
when he went in as a spy.
eighty-five now,
after forty-five years of waiting.

and he doesn't ask
for the easy valley.

he asks for the hill country,
the walled towns, the giants.

I'm as strong now
as I was then, he says.

he followed the LORD
wholeheartedly.

that's what it looks like
at eighty-five.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the low road through the valley in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “that's what it looks like at eighty-five” (Joshua 14:6–14)?

paintings.title: springs of water
paintings.epigraph: “Give me a blessing.”
paintings.poem:
you gave me dry land,
Achsah said to her father.

give me springs of water too.

so he gave her
the upper springs
and the lower springs.

it is not greedy
to ask a father
for water.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Joshua 15:16–19, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “springs of water”—and ends with, “it is not greedy to ask a father for water.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: cities of refuge
paintings.epigraph: “Assign the cities of refuge”
paintings.poem:
six cities
with open gates.

for the one who did harm
without meaning to,
running with his heart in his throat.

get inside, God said.
tell the elders at the gate.
they will take you in.

even in the law
there were doors
left open
for the ones
who didn't mean it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Joshua 20:1–6 points us to the open threshold and whispers, “even in the law there were doors left open for the ones who didn't mean it.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: as for me and my house
paintings.epigraph: “choose today whom you will serve”
paintings.poem:
the gods beyond the river.
the gods of the land.
or the LORD.

choose, he said.
today.

not someday.
not when the harvest is in.

he was an old man
standing in front of a nation,
and he made his own choice
out loud:

as for me
and my house,
we will serve the LORD.

a house is where
it gets decided.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “a house is where it gets decided.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the stone heard
paintings.epigraph: “it has heard all Yahweh’s words”
paintings.poem:
he set up a great stone
under the oak.

this stone has heard
everything God said to us,
he told them.

a strange witness.

it would never speak.
never move.
never forget.

just stand there,
year after year,
in case anyone
needed reminding.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “just stand there, year after year, in case anyone needed reminding” (Joshua 24:26–27) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: Joseph's bones
paintings.epigraph: “They buried the bones of Joseph, which the children of Israel brought up out of Egypt, in Shechem”
paintings.poem:
Joshua died,
a hundred and ten years old.

and they buried
one more thing.

a box of bones
carried all the way
out of Egypt,
through the sea,
through forty years of sand,
across the river.

Joseph had asked them
not to leave him there.

they didn't.

every promise
comes home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “Joseph's bones” (Joshua 24:29–32): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “Joseph had asked them not to leave him there. every promise comes home”?

paintings.title: who didn't know
paintings.epigraph: “another generation arose after them who didn’t know Yahweh”
paintings.poem:
the ones who had seen it
grew old.
the ones who had crossed the river
were buried.

and the stones
were still there.

but no one asked
what they meant.

forgetting
doesn't take a rebellion.

only
one generation
that isn't told.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Judges 2:7–10 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “only one generation that isn't told” in your own story?

paintings.title: round again
paintings.epigraph: “for it grieved Yahweh because of their groaning”
paintings.poem:
they forgot.
they turned to other gods.
they were crushed.
they cried out.

God raised up a judge,
and the land had rest.

then the judge died,
and they forgot.

around and around,
like a donkey at the mill.

the wonder isn't
that they kept circling.
it's that every time they groaned
it grieved him,

and every time,
he came.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “round again” (Judges 2:11–19), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “round again” after reading, “it's that every time they groaned it grieved him, and every time, he came”?

paintings.title: under the palm tree
paintings.epigraph: “She lived under Deborah’s palm tree between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim”
paintings.poem:
no palace.
no throne.

a palm tree
on a hill road
between two towns.

and the people
kept walking up
to sit in its shade
and ask her
what was right.

a prophet,
a judge,
and later she would call herself
a mother in Israel.

wisdom doesn't need a hall.
it can sit
under a tree.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“no palace. no throne”) and the closing thought (“a prophet, a judge, and later she would call herself a mother in Israel. it can sit under a tree”), what is Judges 4:4–5 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: if you will go with me
paintings.epigraph: “Hasn’t Yahweh gone out before you?”
paintings.poem:
if you'll go with me,
I'll go, Barak said.

if not,
I won't.

she went.

and when the day came
she didn't tell him
to be brave.

she told him
who was already
out in front.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Be Strong and Courageous, “if you will go with me” (Judges 4:6–14) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “if you will go with me” to remind us: “she told him who was already out in front.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: a jug of milk
paintings.epigraph: “He asked for water. She gave him milk. She brought him butter in a lordly dish.”
paintings.poem:
he came running
to a tent that looked safe.

he asked for water.
she gave him milk in her best dish
and covered him with a rug.

the captain of nine hundred iron chariots
came to a tent
and never left it.

Deborah had said
it would be a woman's hand.

the song calls her
blessed among women in the tent.

we will leave the rest
in the dark of the tent.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “a jug of milk” (Judges 5:24–25), what would you talk about after reading, “we will leave the rest in the dark of the tent”?

paintings.title: the stars fought
paintings.epigraph: “From the sky the stars fought.”
paintings.poem:
nine hundred chariots of iron.

and then the clouds poured water,
and the ancient river Kishon
swept them away.

from the sky
the stars fought,
Deborah sang.

when God goes out before you,
even the rain
is under orders.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the moving water: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “the stars fought”—“when God goes out before you, even the rain is under orders”?

paintings.title: like the sun
paintings.epigraph: “let those who love him be as the sun when it rises in its strength.”
paintings.poem:
the song ends
not with the battle
but with the morning.

those who love him
will be like the sun
when it comes up
in its strength.

not a flash.
not a fire.

steady.
rising.
warming everything
it touches.

and the land had rest
forty years.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the warmth of the fire in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “and the land had rest forty years” (Judges 5:31)?

paintings.title: in the winepress
paintings.epigraph: “His son Gideon was beating out wheat in the wine press, to hide it from the Midianites.”
paintings.poem:
wheat belongs
on a threshing floor,
in the open,
in the wind.

Gideon was threshing
in a hole in the rock,
where no one could see.

that's where the angel
found him.

and called him
mighty man of valor.

God names you
by what he sees coming,
not by where
you're hiding.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Judges 6:11–12, the story turns on the name by which He calls you—and ends with, “God names you by what he sees coming, not by where you're hiding.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: the least
paintings.epigraph: “I am the least in my father’s house.”
paintings.poem:
if God is with us,
why all this?
where are the wonders
our fathers told us about?

honest questions.
God didn't scold them.

my clan is the poorest.
I'm the least in my house.

God didn't argue that either.

he only said,
I will be with you.

that was the answer
to every one
of Gideon's objections.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Judges 6:13–16 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “the least” and whispers, “that was the answer to every one of Gideon's objections.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: the LORD is peace
paintings.epigraph: “Peace be to you! Don’t be afraid. You shall not die.”
paintings.poem:
he had seen the angel of the LORD
face to face,
and he was sure
that was the end of him.

peace, God said.
don't be afraid.
you won't die.

so he built an altar
right there
and named it
the LORD is peace.

a scared man
naming a stone
after the first thing
God told him.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “a scared man naming a stone after the first thing God told him.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the fleece
paintings.epigraph: “wrung the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.”
paintings.poem:
wet fleece,
dry ground.
he wrung it out
and filled a bowl.

then he asked again.
don't be angry with me.
just once more.

dry fleece,
wet ground.

God did so,
the text says.
no lecture. no thunder.

just dew, exactly where
a frightened man
needed it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “just dew, exactly where a frightened man needed it” (Judges 6:36–40) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: too many
paintings.epigraph: “The people who are with you are too many for me”
paintings.poem:
thirty-two thousand.
too many.

let the fearful go home.
ten thousand.
still too many.

down to the water.
three hundred.

not because God needed
fewer men.

because he wanted
no one to say afterward,
we did this ourselves.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “too many” (Judges 7:2–7): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “because he wanted no one to say afterward, we did this ourselves”?

paintings.title: torches in jars
paintings.epigraph: “empty pitchers, with torches within the pitchers.”
paintings.poem:
a trumpet in one hand.
a clay jar in the other,
and a fire
hidden inside it.

in the middle of the night
they stood around the camp
and broke the jars.

three hundred small lights
blazing all at once.

every man stood in his place.
they didn't have to do more.

sometimes the light
only gets out
when the jar
breaks.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Judges 7:16–21 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “sometimes the light only gets out when the jar breaks” in your own story?

paintings.title: the trees choose a king
paintings.epigraph: “The trees set out to anoint a king over themselves.”
paintings.poem:
the trees wanted a king.

the olive said, and leave my oil?
the fig said, and leave my sweetness?
the vine said, and leave my wine?

each one busy
with the good thing
it was made to give.

so they asked the bramble.
come, it said,
rest in my shade.

a thornbush
has no shade.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “the trees choose a king” (Judges 9:7–15), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the deep roots of the tree after reading, “so they asked the bramble. a thornbush has no shade”?

paintings.title: with tambourines
paintings.epigraph: “the daughters of Israel went yearly to celebrate the daughter of Jephthah”
paintings.poem:
a rash promise
made at the edge of a war.

when he came home,
his only child ran out the door
dancing, with tambourines.

this is one of the hardest pages
in the book.

she asked for two months
on the mountains with her friends.

and every year after,
the daughters of Israel
went out for four days
to remember her.

some stories we can't explain.
we can only refuse to forget
the one who was hurt.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“a rash promise made at the edge of a war”) and the closing thought (“we can only refuse to forget the one who was hurt”), what is Judges 11:30–40 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: a name too wonderful
paintings.epigraph: “Why do you ask about my name, since it is incomprehensible?”
paintings.poem:
what's your name,
Manoah asked,
so we can honor you?

why ask, came the answer.
it's beyond you.

then the flame went up
from the rock,
and the angel went up
in the flame.

we're going to die,
said Manoah.

no, said his wife.
if he wanted us dead
he wouldn't have told us
all this.

sometimes faith
is the one in the room
who reasons it through.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of Be Strong and Courageous, “a name too wonderful” (Judges 13:15–23) slows us down at the name by which He calls you to remind us: “sometimes faith is the one in the room who reasons it through.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: out of the strong
paintings.epigraph: “Out of the strong came out sweetness.”
paintings.poem:
he found honey
where no one would look.

inside the thing
that had roared at him.

he ate it walking,
and gave some to his parents,
and never said
where it came from.

out of the eater, food.
out of the strong, sweetness.

that riddle is bigger
than the man who told it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “out of the strong” (Judges 14:8–14), what would you talk about after reading, “that riddle is bigger than the man who told it”?

paintings.title: but he didn't know
paintings.epigraph: “However, the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaved.”
paintings.poem:
I'll go out like before,
he said,
and shake myself free.

but he didn't know
the LORD had left him.

that's the saddest line
in his story.

they took his eyes.
they put him at the mill
in bronze chains,
grinding in circles.

and then this,
quiet as anything:

his hair
began to grow again.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the loosened chain: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “but he didn't know”—“and then this, quiet as anything: his hair began to grow again”?

paintings.title: remember me
paintings.epigraph: “remember me, please, and strengthen me, please, only this once”
paintings.poem:
he asked the boy
who held his hand
to let him feel the pillars.

a man who had once
torn gates from a city
now needing help
to find a wall.

and then he prayed.
the first real prayer
we hear from him
in a long time.

remember me.
please.
just once more.

and God
remembered him.

paintings.title: in his own eyes
paintings.epigraph: “Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.”
paintings.poem:
no king in Israel.

everyone did
what seemed right
to them.

that's how the book ends.
not with a battle.
with a sentence.

and the long wait begins
for a king
who would do
what was right
in God's eyes.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Judges 21:25, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “in his own eyes”—and ends with, “and the long wait begins for a king who would do what was right in God's eyes.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?
